intro: A Spanish jester sings at dawn, strumming between the verses. Ravel turns the piano into a guitar in Alborada del gracioso, then lets a lonely, unaccompanied voice interrupt the dance.

sections.label: A · Dry guitar chords
sections.mNote: Tightly rolled chords and repeated notes drive the dance

sections.label: B · The jester sings alone
sections.mNote: Plus lent: a bare melody answered by strummed chords

sections.label: Link · The bass settles on A
sections.mNote: The dance pulse returns over a repeated A

sections.label: A′ · Dry chords over E♭
sections.mNote: The opening strums return at ppp in a new key

sections.label: Coda · Staccato chords and the final rush
sections.mNote: Quiet chords gather speed towards the D-major ending

cues.title: A guitar with hammers
cues.text: The piano strums: tightly rolled chords, marked sec, dry, with sharp bass notes underneath. Ravel sets the dance in 6/8 but keeps interrupting its step. The title promises a dawn song from a Spanish jester.
cues.evidence: Miroirs, Demets edition (1906), p. 31: Assez vif, mf sec, les arpèges très serrés. Guitar imitation and the title: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329. Score: https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs,DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One key, many fingers
cues.text: The right hand hammers a repeated note at extraordinary speed, with little scales darting away from it. The left hand keeps a spare accompaniment underneath. A guitar’s repeated pluck becomes a test of the piano’s quick-returning keys.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 33–34: rapid repeated-note passages and short scales; the technique is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The jester’s solitary song
cues.text: The dance stops under a fermata. A single melody follows, Plus lent and expressif en récit, like someone speaking in song. The left hand is silent. Strummed chords keep interrupting at the old tempo.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 35: fermata, Plus lent, 3/4 recitative and alternating 1er Mouvement chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A jester for a critic
cues.text: Ravel dedicates this movement to Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi, the critic and musicologist in his circle of friends. In Miroirs, Calvocoressi receives the Spanish jester; Ricardo Viñes receives the sad birds.
cues.evidence: Dedications and Calvocoressi’s profession: https://imslp.org/wiki/Miroirs,_M.43_(Ravel,_Maurice) and https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

cues.title: A underneath the song
cues.text: The song comes down from its high chords and the bass settles on A. Ravel writes sans ralentir, without slowing. The repeated note brings back the dance’s pulse before the dry guitar chords return.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 39, third and fourth systems: p expressif, then repeated A and sans ralentir.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The guitar returns on tiptoe
cues.text: The strummed chords return at ppp, over E♭ in the bass. Ravel wants them very dry and firmly in rhythm. Their quiet start leaves room for the repeated notes and glissandos that follow.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 39–40: ppp, très sec et bien rythmé, E♭ bass and subsequent glissandos. The E♭ return is also described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The jester keeps dancing
cues.text: Another dry chord stops under a fermata. This time quiet staccato chords follow over low repeated notes. The song stays away: the piano gathers itself for a final rush to D major, with no slowing at the end.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 41–43: sec. fermata chord, pp staccato passage and final sans ralentir. The D-major close is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A fermata leaves one voice
transitions.how: The dance reaches a fortissimo chord and stops under a fermata. Ravel changes to 3/4 and Plus lent: one unaccompanied line sings expressif en récit. The strummed chords return between its phrases at 1er Mouvement.

transitions.title: The song descends to A
transitions.to: Link · The bass settles on A
transitions.how: The high chords marked ff très expressif descend into a quieter phrase. The piano settles on a repeated A, with sans ralentir above it. The dance pulse resumes as the last notes of the song die away.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 39, first four systems.

transitions.title: A becomes E♭ beneath the strums
transitions.from: Link · The bass settles on A
transitions.how: The repeated A quietens, then the bass moves to E♭ beneath the returning guitar chords. Ravel marks them ppp and très sec et bien rythmé. The harmony moves on towards F♯ as the chords grow louder.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 39–40; E♭–F♯ route described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

transitions.title: Quiet chords after the fermata
transitions.to: Coda · Staccato chords and the final rush
transitions.how: The repeated-note passage ends on a fortissimo chord marked sec., held under a fermata. Quiet staccato chords follow, with low repeated notes in the left hand. Ravel keeps the dance moving into the coda, which eventually closes in D major.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 41, last two systems; D-major close on p. 43.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
